chunks.title: CT vs MRI
chunks.tldr: CT: bone white, fast, radiation — fractures, acute blood, calcification, orbital cellulitis, metal FB. MRI: no radiation, best for visual pathway. T1: fat bright, CSF dark. T2: water bright. Gadolinium shows on T1.
points: CT contrast (iodine): avoid in iodine allergy/renal failure; not needed for blood, bone, FB.
CT finds calcification: meningioma, retinoblastoma.
T1 bright: fat, blood (subacute), contrast, melanin.
Fat suppression: T1 fat-sat + gad (sheath lesions); STIR best for optic neuritis.
FLAIR: dark CSF → periventricular MS plaques.
DWI: acute stroke within minutes.
MRI limits: bone invisible, misses acute bleed, no ferrous objects/pacemakers, claustrophobia.
Pituitary: coronal T1 + contrast. Cavernous sinus: coronal.
chunks.hook: T1 = 'Fat is One' (bright). T2 = 'Water is Two' (bright).

cards.q: Best MRI sequence for intraorbital optic neuritis?
cards.a: STIR (short T1 inversion recovery), plus T1 fat-sat with gadolinium.

cards.q: What does FLAIR do?
cards.a: Suppresses bright CSF on T2 images to show periventricular lesions (e.g. MS plaques).

chunks.title: Angiography options
chunks.tldr: MRA: no contrast, misses tiny/thrombosed aneurysms. CTA: method of choice for aneurysms, safe, quick. MRV/CTV: venous sinus thrombosis. Catheter DSA: gold standard but 1% stroke risk; for equivocal cases.
points: MRA uses flow, adds ~10 min.
CTV needs contrast + radiation; MRV can be non-contrast.
DSA via femoral artery; digital subtraction removes bone.
chunks.hook: Painful 3rd nerve palsy → CTA now.

cards.q: Risk of stroke with conventional catheter angiography?
cards.a: About 1%.

chunks.title: Optic nerve anatomy & VEP
chunks.tldr: ~1.2 million axons; 50 mm long: intraocular 1 mm, intraorbital 25–30 mm, canalicular 6 mm (fixed → vulnerable to trauma), intracranial ~10 mm. ⅓ of fibres serve central 5°. VEP: optic neuropathy → delayed latency + low amplitude.
points: Fibres synapse in LGB (some to pretectal nuclei).
Sheaths: pia, arachnoid, dura (continuous with sclera). CSF in subarachnoid space.
Intraorbital nerve 3–4 mm wide (myelin), slack S-shape.
Long intracranial segment → more vulnerable to pituitary/aneurysm.
VEP: flash or pattern; uses: babies, demyelination, functional loss.
chunks.hook: Optic nerve lengths 1 – 25 – 6 – 10 (in mm, front to back).

cards.q: Which optic nerve segment is fixed to bone?
cards.a: The intracanalicular segment (~6 mm).

cards.q: VEP changes in demyelinating optic neuropathy?
cards.a: Prolonged latency (and reduced amplitude).

chunks.title: Signs of optic neuropathy & field patterns
chunks.tldr: Optic nerve = ↓VA, RAPD, red desaturation, ↓brightness, ↓contrast, field loss. Central scotoma: demyelination, toxic, LHON, compression. Altitudinal: AION, glaucoma, drusen. Big blind spot: papilloedema.
points: Colour: red–green mainly; compare red target between eyes or Ishihara.
Brightness loss often outlasts VA recovery after neuritis.
Tilted discs: upper temporal defects not respecting the vertical meridian.
Causes: inflammatory, glaucomatous, ischaemic, hereditary, toxic/nutritional, papilloedema, trauma, compressive, infiltrative.
chunks.hook: Red goes pink in a sick nerve.

cards.q: Field defect respecting the horizontal meridian from the optic nerve?
cards.a: Altitudinal – AION (also glaucoma, disc drusen).

chunks.title: Optic atrophy types
chunks.tldr: Primary: flat white, sharp margins (neuritis, compression, hereditary, toxic, trauma). Secondary: after swelling — grey, blurred, gliosis, Paton lines. Consecutive: from retinal disease — waxy (RP, PRP, CRAO). Band/bow-tie: chiasm/tract.
points: Fewer small vessels on disc (Kestenbaum sign), thin RNFL.
Temporal pallor: papillomacular bundle (MS, toxic/nutritional).
Band atrophy: nasal + temporal fibres (from the temporal field of the contralateral eye) — chiasm or tract.
Unilateral = before chiasm; bilateral = chiasm/tract.
chunks.hook: Primary = Plain. Secondary = Scarred. Consecutive = Comes from retina.

cards.q: Causes of secondary optic atrophy?
cards.a: Previous disc swelling: chronic papilloedema, AION, papillitis.

chunks.title: Optic neuritis types & MS link
chunks.tldr: Retrobulbar (normal disc, adults, MS), papillitis (kids), neuroretinitis (macular star, rarely MS). MS after ON: ~50% at 15 yrs; 25% if MRI normal, >70% if lesions.
points: Causes: demyelinating (most), parainfectious, infectious, non-infectious (sarcoid, SLE, vasculitis).
Other demyelination: NMO/Devic (aquaporin-4 antibodies, bilateral ON + transverse myelitis); Schilder (kids, fatal).
MS: women, 20s–40s; Lhermitte, Uhthoff (worse with heat/exercise).
Eye in MS: ON, INO, nystagmus; rarer skew, palsies, intermediate uveitis, periphlebitis.
CSF oligoclonal bands 90–95%. VEP abnormal ~100% definite MS.
Lower MS risk (normal MRI): male, no viral prodrome, disc swelling/haemorrhage/exudate, NPL, no pain.
ON presenting feature of MS in up to 30%; occurs in 50% with MS.
chunks.hook: MRI decides: clean 25%, spotty 70%.

cards.q: 15-year MS risk after optic neuritis with ≥1 MRI lesion?
cards.a: Over 70% (25% if MRI normal).

cards.q: What is the Uhthoff phenomenon?
cards.a: Worsening of vision/symptoms with heat or exercise in demyelination.

chunks.title: Demyelinating optic neuritis: clinic & treatment
chunks.tldr: Age 20–50, subacute monocular loss + pain on eye movement (>90%), VA 6/18–6/60, RAPD, colour loss. Worsens ≤3 wks, then improves; >90% reach 6/9. Steroids (ONTT): IV methylpred 1 g × 3 d then oral → faster recovery, same final VA. Oral alone ↑ recurrence.
points: Phosphenes; frontal headache.
Disc normal (retrobulbar) in most; fellow eye may show temporal pallor.
Fields: diffuse central depression commonest; also altitudinal, central, centrocaecal.
Residual: colour, brightness, mild RAPD, pallor. ~10% chronic.
Steroid if VA <6/12 in first week, poor other eye.
Regimen: IV 1 g/day × 3 then oral pred 1 mg/kg × 11 days, taper 3 days.
MS drugs: interferon beta / glatiramer (first attack); natalizumab, ocrelizumab (PML risk), alemtuzumab, fingolimod, cladribine for active.
chunks.hook: ONTT: IV speeds it up, oral alone backfires.

cards.q: Effect of IV steroids on final visual outcome in optic neuritis (ONTT)?
cards.a: None – faster recovery only; oral prednisolone alone increased recurrence.

cards.q: Percentage with pain on eye movement in demyelinating optic neuritis?
cards.a: Over 90%.

chunks.title: Other optic neuritis & neuroretinitis
chunks.tldr: Parainfectious: kids, 1–3 wks after virus/vaccine, bilateral papillitis, good recovery. Infectious: sinus, cat-scratch, syphilis, Lyme, cryptococcus, VZV. Sarcoid: lumpy disc, steroid-dependent. Neuroretinitis: disc swelling + macular star; Bartonella 60%.
points: Parainfectious: measles, mumps, chickenpox, rubella, EBV; IV steroid if bilateral severe.
Sinus-related: recurrent, severe headache, spheno-ethmoid; antibiotics/drainage.
Sarcoid ON: relapses on taper; methotrexate adjunct.
Neuroretinitis: painless, mild nerve signs (macular cause of VA loss); star appears as disc settles; recovers over 6–12 m.
Neuroretinitis causes: cat-scratch, idiopathic (Leber stellate) 25%, syphilis, Lyme, mumps, leptospirosis.
chunks.hook: Star at the macula → ask about the cat.

cards.q: Commonest cause of neuroretinitis?
cards.a: Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) ~60%.

cards.q: Typical parainfectious optic neuritis presentation?
cards.a: Child, 1–3 weeks after viral illness, bilateral papillitis with severe loss; good spontaneous recovery.

chunks.title: NAION
chunks.tldr: Short posterior ciliary artery infarct of the disc. >50 yrs, 'disc at risk' (small/no cup), hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnoea, nocturnal hypotension. Painless loss on waking, inferior altitudinal defect, hyperaemic swollen disc. Fellow eye ~15% at 5 yrs.
points: Other risks: lipids, antiphospholipid, homocysteine, hypotension, cataract surgery.
VA normal/near-normal in ~30%.
Colour loss proportional to VA (vs ON: colour worse than VA).
Pallor by 3–6 weeks.
Always exclude GCA (ESR/CRP).
No proven treatment: nerve fenestration useless; aspirin doesn't protect other eye; treat risk factors.
chunks.hook: NAION = crowded disc wakes up blind at the bottom (inferior altitudinal, on waking).

cards.q: Structural risk factor for NAION?
cards.a: Small crowded disc with little or no cup ('disc at risk').

cards.q: Fellow eye risk in NAION?
cards.a: About 10% at 2 years, 15% at 5 years.

chunks.title: Giant cell arteritis: diagnosis
chunks.tldr: >50 (avg 70), women 4×. Scalp tenderness, headache, jaw claudication (pathognomonic), PMR (50%). Tender, thick, pulseless temporal artery. ESR (>60; normal in 20%), CRP, high platelets. Biopsy ≥2.5 cm within ~7 days of steroids — never delay steroids.
points: Granulomatous arteritis of elastic arteries; spares intracranial.
Risks: smoking, low BMI, early menopause.
Systemic: weight loss, fever, sweats; aortic aneurysm/dissection, MI, stroke.
Ocular motor palsies (even pupil-involving III).
ACR criteria (≥3 of 5): age ≥50, new headache, TA tenderness/↓pulse, ESR ≥50, positive biopsy.
Skip lesions → 15% false-negative biopsy; contralateral +5%.
Doppler halo sign (~75%) — valid alternative.
Long-term aortic imaging advised.
chunks.hook: Jaw hurts chewing + old + headache = GCA until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Virtually pathognomonic symptom of GCA?
cards.a: Jaw claudication.

cards.q: Minimum temporal artery biopsy length and why?
cards.a: At least 2.5 cm, because of skip lesions.

chunks.title: Arteritic AION & treatment
chunks.tldr: AAION in 30–50% of untreated GCA; ⅓ get second eye within days. Chalky white swollen disc, severe loss, often preceded by amaurosis fugax. Rx: IV methylpred 0.5–1 g × 3 d → oral 1–2 mg/kg, slow taper + aspirin, bone + gut protection. Aim: save the other eye.
points: Can come with cilioretinal artery occlusion or CRAO (shared trunk).
No-vision-loss GCA: oral pred ~1 mg/kg.
Taper: 50–60 mg for 4 weeks → −10 mg/2 wks to 20 → slow; 1–2 yrs total.
Monitor ESR/CRP (CRP falls faster), BP, glucose, bone density, aortic imaging.
Second eye still lost in up to 25% despite steroids.
Methotrexate steroid-sparing.
Pseudo-Foster Kennedy: AION swelling one eye + old atrophy other. True FK: frontal mass → ipsilateral atrophy + contralateral papilloedema.
chunks.hook: Chalk-white swollen disc = arteritic. Hyperaemic = non-arteritic.

cards.q: Disc appearance suggesting arteritic AION?
cards.a: Pale 'chalky white' oedematous disc.

cards.q: Distinguish pseudo-Foster Kennedy from true Foster Kennedy.
cards.a: Pseudo: sequential AION (old atrophy + new swelling). True: frontal mass → ipsilateral compressive atrophy + contralateral papilloedema.

chunks.title: PION & LHON
chunks.tldr: PION: normal disc then pallor; perioperative (spine/cardiac, anaemia + hypotension, bilateral, poor), arteritic, non-arteritic. LHON: mitochondrial 11778 (ND4), young men 15–35, sequential painless central loss, telangiectatic disc that doesn't leak. Idebenone may help.
points: PION is a diagnosis of exclusion (rule out compression/inflammation).
LHON: maternal inheritance; consider in any bilateral optic neuropathy at any age.
Signs: disc hyperaemia, pseudo-oedema, telangiectatic microangiopathy; pupils surprisingly OK.
Fellow eye within weeks–months; final ≤6/60 typical; 11778 worst; 14484 best.
Carriers may show telangiectasia; OCT thick temporal RNFL in carriers.
FA: no leakage. Fields: central/centrocaecal.
chunks.hook: LHON = Lads Have Optic Nerve loss from Mum.

cards.q: Commonest LHON mutation?
cards.a: m.11778G>A in MT-ND4 (worst prognosis).

cards.q: Main risk factors for perioperative PION?
cards.a: Anaemia and intraoperative hypotension (spine/cardiac surgery).

chunks.title: Other hereditary & nutritional optic neuropathy
chunks.tldr: Dominant optic atrophy (Kjer, OPA1): commonest hereditary (1:50,000), childhood, slow, temporal pallor, 6/12–6/60. Wolfram (DIDMOAD): diabetes first, then severe atrophy. Nutritional (tobacco-alcohol): bilateral centrocaecal scotomas, colour worse than VA → B12, thiamine, folate; stop alcohol/smoking.
points: Kjer: 20% hearing loss.
Behr (AR): optic atrophy + ataxia + spasticity + learning disability.
Wolfram: Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, Deafness; WFS1; short life.
LHON care: avoid smoking/alcohol, idebenone; avoid cyanocobalamin (use hydroxocobalamin).
Nutritional: vegan diet, pernicious anaemia, elderly; also drugs/toxins.
VEP in nutritional: amplitude ↓, latency near normal.
Correct B12 before folate (avoid subacute combined degeneration).
Good prognosis early; colour returns slower than VA.
chunks.hook: DIDMOAD spells Wolfram. Booze + smokes + bad diet = centrocaecal scotomas.

cards.q: Gene in dominant (Kjer) optic atrophy?
cards.a: OPA1.

cards.q: Field defect of nutritional optic neuropathy?
cards.a: Bilateral symmetrical centrocaecal scotomas.

chunks.title: Raised ICP & papilloedema basics
chunks.tldr: Papilloedema = disc swelling from raised ICP — image urgently (mass until proven otherwise). Symptoms: morning headache, vomiting, transient obscurations (seconds, with posture), VI palsy (false localising). Vision usually normal till late. No LP before imaging.
points: CSF: choroid plexus → lateral ventricles → Monro → 3rd → aqueduct → 4th → Luschka/Magendie → subarachnoid → arachnoid villi.
Normal opening pressure 10–18 cmH2O (lying).
Causes: IIH, hydrocephalus, masses/bleeds, meningitis/SAH, venous sinus thrombosis, trauma, malignant hypertension.
SVP present → ICP normal at that moment (but absent in 20% of normals).
B-scan: optic nerve sheath diameter >5–5.7 mm; crescent sign; 30° test (diameter falls 10% on lateral gaze if fluid).
Other disc swelling: malignant HTN, AION, neuritis, infiltration, CRVO, uveitis, hypotony, LHON, methanol.
chunks.hook: Swollen discs = scan first, tap later.

cards.q: Why must imaging precede lumbar puncture in papilloedema?
cards.a: To exclude a mass that could cause herniation (coning) after LP.

cards.q: Significance of spontaneous venous pulsation?
cards.a: If present, ICP is normal at that time (absent in ~20% of normal people).

chunks.title: Papilloedema stages & IIH
chunks.tldr: Stages: early (hyperaemia, blurred margins, cup kept) → established (cup lost, haemorrhages, CWS, Paton lines, macular fan, big blind spot) → chronic (shunts, corpora amylacea) → atrophic. IIH: obese young women, headache, pulsatile tinnitus; MRI empty sella; MRV. Rx: weight loss + acetazolamide.
points: Nearly always bilateral (may be asymmetric).
Macular fan (vesicles) ≠ macular star (exudates).
IIH drugs: OCP, tetracyclines, vitamin A/retinoids; SLE, sleep apnoea.
IIH vision: usually good but 25% some permanent loss.
Other IIH options: furosemide, digoxin; optic nerve sheath fenestration, LP shunt, venous sinus stenting; mannitol/LP for crisis.
Ophthalmologist monitors VA, colour, fields, disc photos.
chunks.hook: IIH = Female, Fat, Fertile-age, Fields to watch.

cards.q: MRI signs of IIH?
cards.a: Empty sella, slit ventricles, distended optic nerve sheaths, transverse sinus stenosis.

cards.q: First-line medical treatment for IIH?
cards.a: Weight loss plus acetazolamide.

chunks.title: Tilted disc, pit & drusen
chunks.tldr: Tilted disc: myopes, oval, situs inversus, superotemporal defect crossing vertical midline. Pit: grey hole (temporal) → serous macular detachment ~50% (age ~30) → check discs in 'CSR'. Drusen: 2%, bilateral 75%; buried in kids = pseudopapilloedema; see on FAF/US; fields lost in 75%.
points: Tilted: ovality index >1.3; GCC on OCT helps exclude glaucoma. Torsional disc >15°.
Pit: field defects mimic glaucoma; schisis then outer detachment; FA doesn't fill it.
Pit maculopathy: observe (25% resolve), laser at temporal disc edge, vitrectomy + gas.
Drusen buried: lumpy, no cup, anomalous branching, no hyperaemia.
Drusen associations: RP, angioid streaks, Alagille (90%).
Drusen complications: AION, CNV, haemorrhage, vascular occlusion.
CT shows calcification but too much radiation just for drusen.
chunks.hook: Pit → puddle at the macula. Drusen glow on FAF.

cards.q: Complication of optic disc pit?
cards.a: Serous macular detachment (schisis-like) in about half of eyes.

cards.q: Best simple test to show buried disc drusen?
cards.a: Fundus autofluorescence (or B-scan ultrasound).

chunks.title: Coloboma, morning glory & hypoplasia
chunks.tldr: Coloboma: inferior white bowl (fissure didn't close) → superior field defect; CHARGE, PAX6. Morning glory: funnel with central glial tuft + spoke vessels; RD 30%; basal encephalocele. Hypoplasia: small disc, double-ring sign; check pituitary (septo-optic dysplasia).
points: Coloboma associations: microphthalmos, iris/lens coloboma; complications RD, CNV.
Morning glory: unilateral, sporadic; frontonasal dysplasia, pituitary problems.
Hypoplasia: young mother, first baby, drugs/alcohol; disc–fovea distance ≥3 disc diameters.
Hypoplasia presents: blind roving eyes (bilateral) or squint (unilateral).
Screen hormones (growth, cortisol, thyroid) + development.
Papillorenal (PAX2): excavated disc + kidney disease. Megalopapilla: big disc, normal rim.
Peripapillary staphyloma: normal disc deep in a hole, poor VA.
chunks.hook: Morning glory flower: white centre, petals = radial vessels.

cards.q: What is the double-ring sign?
cards.a: Pale scleral ring with pigment border around a small disc – optic nerve hypoplasia.

cards.q: Must-do investigation in optic nerve hypoplasia?
cards.a: Endocrine (pituitary) and neurodevelopmental screening; MRI brain.

chunks.title: Myelinated fibres & disc vessels
chunks.tldr: Myelinated nerve fibres: white feathery patches (1%), myopia/anisometropia → amblyopia. Aicardi: girls, chorioretinal lacunae, CNS defects (XLD). Collaterals (after RVO), optociliary shunts (optic nerve sheath meningioma), disc NV.
points: MNF: absolute scotoma; ⅔ not touching disc; 5–10% bilateral.
Aicardi: infantile spasms, corpus callosum agenesis; lethal in boys.
Optociliary shunt: retina-to-choroid; vessels vanish at disc edge.
Classic triad of ONSM: visual loss + disc pallor + shunt vessels.
chunks.hook: Shunt vessels + pale disc + slow vision loss = sheath meningioma.

cards.q: Most common cause of optociliary shunt vessels?
cards.a: Optic nerve sheath meningioma (also CRVO, glioma, papilloedema).

chunks.title: Light reflex pathway & RAPD
chunks.tldr: 4 neurones: retina → pretectal nuclei (both) → Edinger–Westphal (both) → III (inferior division, via nerve to IO) → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nerves → sphincter. RAPD: swing light — affected eye's pupils dilate. Afferent problems = equal pupils.
points: Internuncial (pretectal → EW) damage = light–near dissociation (neurosyphilis, pinealoma).
Only parasympathetic fibres synapse in the ciliary ganglion.
Near reflex = accommodation + convergence + miosis; no disease has light reflex without near.
Absolute (amaurotic) pupil: NPL eye, no direct response, normal consensual.
RAPD: incomplete optic nerve or severe retinal disease; never dense cataract.
Anisocoria = efferent or iris problem.
chunks.hook: Afferent = Alike pupils. Anisocoria = Arm (efferent) problem.

cards.q: Does a dense cataract cause an RAPD?
cards.a: No.

cards.q: Where do parasympathetic pupil fibres synapse?
cards.a: Ciliary ganglion.

chunks.title: Horner syndrome
chunks.tldr: Ptosis 1–2 mm + miosis + (anhidrosis); anisocoria worse in the dark (dilation lag). 3 neurones: hypothalamus → C8–T2 (Budge) → superior cervical ganglion (past lung apex) → along ICA → V1 → long ciliary nerves. Painful acute Horner = carotid dissection → urgent imaging.
points: Inverse ptosis of lower lid; light/near reactions normal.
Congenital/long-standing: lighter iris (heterochromia).
Anhidrosis only if lesion below superior cervical ganglion (face sweat fibres follow external carotid).
Central: Wallenberg stroke, syrinx, MS. Preganglionic: Pancoast, neck surgery, aneurysm. Postganglionic: ICA dissection, cavernous sinus, nasopharyngeal ca, cluster headache.
Imaging: CTA/MRA aortic arch → circle of Willis.
Check T1 (grip), lymph nodes, cranial nerves.
chunks.hook: Horner = 'PAM': Ptosis, Anhidrosis, Miosis. Pain + Horner = dissection.

cards.q: Why is Horner anisocoria greater in dim light?
cards.a: The Horner pupil dilates poorly/slowly (dilation lag) while the normal pupil dilates.

cards.q: Urgent cause to exclude in acute painful Horner syndrome?
cards.a: Internal carotid artery dissection.

chunks.title: Horner drop tests
chunks.tldr: Confirm: apraclonidine — Horner pupil dilates (reversal of anisocoria; upregulated α1). Cocaine 4% — normal dilates, Horner doesn't. Localise: hydroxyamphetamine / phenylephrine 1% — postganglionic Horner fails to dilate with hydroxyamphetamine but dilates with phenylephrine (hypersensitivity).
points: Apraclonidine: check at 30–45 min; sensitivity ~90%, specificity ~100%; may be negative in first ~2 weeks; not in infants.
Cocaine: blocks noradrenaline reuptake; anisocoria ≥0.8 mm significant; good for acute cases.
Wait 3–5 days between tests (apraclonidine lasts).
Hydroxyamphetamine releases NA from intact 3rd neurone.
chunks.hook: Apraclonidine flips it; cocaine shows it; hydroxyamphetamine places it.

cards.q: Mechanism of apraclonidine test in Horner?
cards.a: Denervation upregulates α1 receptors in dilator pupillae → Horner pupil dilates.

cards.q: Hydroxyamphetamine: no dilation of the Horner pupil means?
cards.a: Postganglionic (third-order) lesion.

chunks.title: Adie tonic pupil
chunks.tldr: Young woman, big pupil, poor light reaction, slow tonic near response, vermiform iris movements. Ciliary ganglion damage (post-viral). Dilute pilocarpine 0.1% constricts it (denervation hypersensitivity). + absent knee jerks = Holmes–Adie.
points: Unilateral 80%; other eye often later.
Accommodation also tonic → near blur.
Old Adie becomes small.
Ross syndrome: + sweating abnormalities.
Bilateral tonic pupils → check syphilis serology.
Rx: reading glasses, sunglasses, dilute pilocarpine.
chunks.hook: Adie = Aching for near (slow), Absent reflexes, Accepts weak pilocarpine.

cards.q: Diagnostic drop for Adie pupil?
cards.a: Pilocarpine 0.1–0.125% – the Adie pupil constricts, the normal doesn't.

cards.q: What is Holmes–Adie syndrome?
cards.a: Adie tonic pupil with reduced deep tendon reflexes.

chunks.title: Other pupil oddities & light–near dissociation
chunks.tldr: Physiological anisocoria (~20%, ≤1 mm, same in light & dark). Pharmacological mydriasis: huge, no response even to 1% pilocarpine. Argyll Robertson (syphilis): small irregular, near yes, light no. Tectal pupils: mid-dilated, LND. BEUM: young women, minutes–hours.
points: Pharmacological: scopolamine patch, someone else's drops, malingering.
AR pupils: don't dilate in dark; no response to 0.1% pilocarpine (vs bilateral old Adie).
Light–near dissociation unilateral: afferent defect, Adie, HZO, aberrant III regeneration.
Bilateral: neurosyphilis, diabetes, myotonic dystrophy, Parinaud, amyloid, encephalitis, alcoholism.
BEUM: 0.1% pilo no effect, 1% pilo constricts.
chunks.hook: Argyll Robertson = Accommodates, doesn't React (like a prostitute: accommodates but doesn't react).

cards.q: Dilated pupil not constricting to 1% pilocarpine?
cards.a: Pharmacological mydriasis (atropinic block).

cards.q: Features of Argyll Robertson pupils?
cards.a: Small, irregular, bilateral; constrict to near but not light; neurosyphilis.

chunks.title: Chiasm anatomy & field patterns
chunks.tldr: Chiasm sits above the pituitary (diaphragma sellae) → field loss = suprasellar extension. Inferonasal fibres cross low/front → pituitary gives superotemporal first → bitemporal hemianopia. Craniopharyngioma (from above) → inferotemporal first. Anterior chiasm lesion → junctional scotoma.
points: 80% chiasm directly over sella; 10% prefixed (tract lesions), 10% postfixed (optic nerve/junction lesions).
Microadenoma <10 mm stays in sella.
Cavernous sinus lateral (III, IV, VI, V1, V2); ICA below optic nerves; ACA above.
Junctional scotoma: central defect one eye + superotemporal defect other (Wilbrand's knee).
Posterior chiasm: central bitemporal defects (macular fibres cross posteriorly).
Early sign: red desaturation across the vertical midline.
Band/bow-tie atrophy in ~50% with field loss → guarded recovery.
Postfixation blindness: trouble threading needles; hemifield slide → diplopia.
Mimics: tilted discs, nasal RP/schisis, dermatochalasis, functional.
chunks.hook: Pituitary pushes up → top (superior) fields go first. Cranio presses down → bottom fields first.

cards.q: Which quadrants are lost first in pituitary adenoma?
cards.a: Superotemporal (bitemporal superior quadrantanopia).

cards.q: What is a junctional scotoma?
cards.a: Central scotoma in one eye with a contralateral superotemporal defect, from a lesion at the optic nerve–chiasm junction.

chunks.title: Pituitary adenomas & apoplexy
chunks.tldr: Prolactinoma commonest (amenorrhoea–galactorrhoea, impotence) → cabergoline/bromocriptine. GH → acromegaly; ACTH → Cushing. 25% non-secreting (present with vision). Surgery: trans-sphenoidal. Apoplexy: thunderclap headache + vision loss + ophthalmoplegia + Addisonian crisis → emergency.
points: Anterior pituitary: GH, FSH, LH, PRL, TSH, ACTH. Posterior: ADH, oxytocin.
MRI with gadolinium (coronal + sagittal).
Headache without raised-ICP features; papilloedema rare.
Octreotide for GH tumours.
Field recovery fastest in first weeks after surgery.
Radiotherapy rarely (stereotactic).
Sheehan syndrome: postpartum pituitary infarct.
Apoplexy needs steroids, MRI, urgent fields, ± decompression.
chunks.hook: Pituitary apoplexy = 'stroke of the sella': headache + blind + double + crash (cortisol).

cards.q: Most common pituitary adenoma and first-line treatment?
cards.a: Prolactinoma – dopamine agonist (cabergoline).

cards.q: Life-threatening systemic danger in pituitary apoplexy?
cards.a: Acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis – give steroids.

chunks.title: Craniopharyngioma & meningiomas
chunks.tldr: Craniopharyngioma: Rathke pouch, kids (dwarfism, delayed puberty, obesity) + adults (vision); calcified, cystic; inferotemporal defects first. Meningioma: middle-aged women; tuberculum sellae → junctional scotoma; sphenoid ridge → temporal fullness (hyperostosis); olfactory groove → anosmia.
points: Craniopharyngioma: solid part isointense T1, cysts bright T1; surgery, recurrences common.
Lateral sphenoid ridge: late optic nerve involvement; medial: early.
Foster Kennedy: olfactory groove/frontal mass.
Meningioma: surgery ± radiotherapy, or observe.
chunks.hook: Cranio = Calcified, Cystic, Child.

cards.q: Typical first field defect of craniopharyngioma?
cards.a: Bitemporal inferior quadrantanopia (compression from above).

chunks.title: Optic tract & radiations
chunks.tldr: Behind the chiasm = homonymous defects; further back = more congruous. Tract: incongruous + RAPD (contralateral) + optic atrophy (bow-tie in contralateral eye). Temporal (Meyer loop): 'pie in the sky'. Parietal: 'pie on the floor' + asymmetric OKN.
points: Wernicke hemianopic pupil: light from blind side → no response (hard to do).
Tract lesion + cerebral peduncle → contralateral pyramidal signs.
Radiations (3rd-order from LGB) → no optic atrophy.
Temporal lobe: uncinate fits, formed hallucinations, receptive dysphasia (dominant).
Parietal: dominant → Gerstmann (acalculia, agraphia, L–R confusion, finger agnosia); non-dominant → neglect, dressing apraxia.
Cogan: parietal (tumour) = OKN poor towards lesion side; occipital (infarct) = symmetrical OKN.
chunks.hook: PITS: Parietal Inferior, Temporal Superior.

cards.q: Field defect from a temporal lobe (Meyer loop) lesion?
cards.a: Contralateral superior homonymous quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky').

cards.q: Which retrochiasmal lesion causes optic atrophy and RAPD?
cards.a: Optic tract lesion.

chunks.title: Occipital cortex & higher visual syndromes
chunks.tldr: PCA stroke (>90% of isolated homonymous hemianopia) → congruous, macular-sparing (macula has MCA backup). Occipital tip trauma → congruous macular defects. Anterior calcarine → temporal crescent. Anton: denies blindness. Riddoch: sees only motion.
points: Others: trauma, tumour, migraine (rare), PML, CJD.
Benson (posterior cortical atrophy): visual Alzheimer — normal eyes, agnosia, alexia.
Balint: simultanagnosia + optic ataxia + ocular apraxia (parieto-occipital).
PRES: malignant HTN, eclampsia, tacrolimus/ciclosporin → cortical blindness, seizures; reversible.
AZOOR can mimic hemianopia.
chunks.hook: Macular sparing = Occipital stroke (two blood supplies).

cards.q: Why is the macula spared in occipital infarcts?
cards.a: Macular cortex has dual supply from posterior and middle cerebral arteries.

cards.q: What is Anton syndrome?
cards.a: Cortical blindness with denial of blindness.

chunks.title: Third nerve anatomy & brainstem syndromes
chunks.tldr: Nucleus in midbrain (superior colliculus level). Levator = one midline subnucleus (bilateral ptosis); SR subnucleus supplies the OTHER eye. Fascicular: Weber (peduncle → contralateral hemiparesis), Benedikt (red nucleus → tremor), Nothnagel (ataxia), Claude (both).
points: Nuclear III: bilateral ptosis + contralateral SR weakness.
WEBINO: bilateral MR subnuclei.
Basilar course: between PCA and SCA, alongside PComm → PComm aneurysm.
Uncal herniation: irritative miosis → fixed dilated pupil → full III.
Cavernous: lateral wall above IV; with IV, VI, V1 → diabetes, apoplexy, aneurysm, CCF, Tolosa–Hunt.
Superior division: levator + SR. Inferior: MR, IR, IO + pupil fibres (via nerve to IO).
chunks.hook: Weber = Weak body. Benedikt = Bobbing (tremor). Nothnagel = No balance.

cards.q: Third nerve palsy + contralateral hemiparesis?
cards.a: Weber syndrome (cerebral peduncle).

cards.q: Why does a nuclear 3rd nerve lesion cause bilateral ptosis?
cards.a: A single midline levator subnucleus supplies both levators.

chunks.title: Third nerve palsy: pupil rule & management
chunks.tldr: 'Down and out', ptosis, dilated pupil. Pupil fibres are superficial (pial supply) → compression involves pupil; microvascular (vasa nervorum) spares pupil (80%). Pupil-involving III = urgent CTA (PComm aneurysm). Aberrant regeneration → never microvascular.
points: Microvascular ~40% of isolated III; pain common (doesn't exclude aneurysm).
Aneurysm: pupil involvement out of proportion to motility.
Rule isn't perfect: pupil may become involved days later.
Trivial trauma causing III → suspect aneurysm/tumour.
Aberrant regeneration (trauma/compression): lid lifts on adduction/downgaze (pseudo-Graefe), pupil constricts on adduction.
Others: tumour, syphilis, Lyme, sarcoid, GCA; myasthenia mimics.
Ix: vascular risks, CTA urgently if suspicious, MRI ± MRV.
Rx: observe (recovers weeks–months), occlusion/prisms; botox to LR; surgery after 6–12 months.
chunks.hook: Pupil out = Pressure (surgical). Pupil spared = Poor vessels (medical).

cards.q: Why are pupillary fibres affected by compressive third nerve lesions?
cards.a: They lie superficially (superomedially) and are supplied by pial vessels.

cards.q: Significance of aberrant regeneration of the third nerve?
cards.a: Implies trauma or compression (aneurysm/tumour), not microvascular ischaemia.

chunks.title: Fourth nerve palsy
chunks.tldr: Longest, thinnest, only dorsal exit, crosses (nucleus supplies contralateral SO). Causes: congenital decompensated (large vertical fusion range, old photos with head tilt), trauma (often bilateral), microvascular. Signs: hypertropia worse on opposite gaze + same-side tilt; head tilts away.
points: Fewest axons of any cranial nerve.
Decussates in anterior medullary velum → hit by tentorium in trauma.
Head posture: tilt to opposite side, chin down, face turn opposite.
Parks 3-step: which eye high → worse on which gaze → worse on which tilt. SO palsy: WOOG (worse on opposite gaze) + BOOT (better on opposite tilt).
Bilateral: alternating hyper on side gaze, >10° excyclotorsion, V-pattern eso, bilateral positive Bielschowsky.
Imaging only if not improving.
Surgery: <15 Δ IO weakening or SO tuck; bigger add SR/contralateral IR; Harada–Ito for torsion.
chunks.hook: WOOG & BOOT — Worse On Opposite Gaze, Better On Opposite Tilt.

cards.q: Signs of bilateral fourth nerve palsy?
cards.a: Excyclotorsion >10°, V-pattern esotropia, alternating hypertropia, bilateral positive head tilt.

cards.q: What is the Harada–Ito procedure?
cards.a: Anterolateral transposition of the anterior (lateral) half of the SO tendon to correct excyclotorsion.

chunks.title: Sixth nerve palsy
chunks.tldr: Esotropia worse at distance, poor abduction, face turns towards the palsy. Nuclear lesion = gaze palsy (+ VII) — isolated VI is never nuclear. Basilar causes: acoustic neuroma (check hearing + corneal reflex), raised ICP (false localising), skull fracture, Gradenigo. Kids/bilateral → urgent imaging.
points: Foville (dorsal pons): VI–VIII, Horner, gaze palsy. Millard–Gubler (ventral): VI + VII + contralateral hemiplegia. Raymond: VI + contralateral hemiplegia.
Course: over petrous tip through Dorello canal into cavernous sinus (most medial, beside ICA).
Cavernous VI + Horner = Parkinson sign.
Gradenigo: petrous apicitis → VI palsy + facial pain (V) + deafness.
Microvascular common in older adults (up to 60%); congenital decompensation rare.
Up to 90% recover in weeks–months; alternate patch kids.
Botox to ipsilateral MR. Surgery ≥6–12 m: partial → MR recession + LR resection; complete → vertical rectus transposition + MR weakening (not 3 recti at once).
chunks.hook: VI palsy? Ask 'Can you hear me?' and touch the cornea.

cards.q: Two bedside tests in every 6th nerve palsy?
cards.a: Hearing and corneal sensation (to exclude vestibular schwannoma).

cards.q: What is Gradenigo syndrome?
cards.a: Petrous apex inflammation (mastoiditis) causing VI palsy, facial pain and hearing loss.

chunks.title: Gaze control, INO & one-and-a-half
chunks.tldr: Saccades: frontal eye field → contralateral PPRF. Pursuit: ipsilateral. PPRF → VI nucleus + (via crossed MLF) contralateral MR. INO = MLF: poor adduction on lesion side + abducting nystagmus other eye. One-and-a-half: PPRF + MLF same side → only contralateral abduction left.
points: PPRF lesion: can't look towards the lesion side.
INO named for the side of the adduction deficit; convergence spared if anterior/discrete.
Causes: young = MS (often bilateral); old = stroke.
WEBINO: bilateral INO + exotropia (rostral midbrain).
Doll's eye (vestibular) reflex tests supranuclear vs nuclear.
chunks.hook: INO: the eye on the bad side can't go In (to the nose).

cards.q: Lesion site in internuclear ophthalmoplegia?
cards.a: Medial longitudinal fasciculus (ipsilateral to the adduction deficit).

cards.q: Only movement preserved in one-and-a-half syndrome?
cards.a: Abduction of the contralateral eye (with nystagmus).

chunks.title: Parinaud, PSP & skew
chunks.tldr: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain): upgaze palsy, light–near dissociation, Collier lid retraction, convergence–retraction nystagmus. Kids: pinealoma, aqueduct stenosis. PSP: elderly, downgaze first, falls, rigidity. Skew: vertical misalignment from brainstem/cerebellar stroke.
points: Vertical gaze centre: rostral interstitial nucleus of MLF (midbrain).
Parinaud: doll's head downgaze intact (supranuclear).
Young adults: MS, trauma, AVM; elderly: stroke, masses, aneurysm.
PSP (Steele–Richardson–Olszewski): then horizontal palsy, pseudobulbar palsy, dementia.
chunks.hook: Parinaud = can't look Up, pupils don't light Up, lids pulled Up.

cards.q: Features of Parinaud syndrome?
cards.a: Upgaze palsy, light–near dissociation, Collier sign, convergence–retraction nystagmus.

cards.q: Which gaze is lost first in PSP?
cards.a: Downgaze (vertical).

chunks.title: Nystagmus basics & physiological types
chunks.tldr: Jerk (slow drift + fast correction; named by fast phase) vs pendular (equal speeds). Physiological: end-point, OKN, vestibular. Calorics: COWS — Cold Opposite, Warm Same. Both ears cold → fast up; warm → fast down.
points: Describe plane, amplitude, frequency.
OKN drum right→left: left parietal = pursuit left; left frontal = saccade right.
OKN uses: babies' vision, functional blindness, hemianopia localisation.
Peripheral vestibular: unidirectional, dampened by fixation, worse looking towards fast phase (Alexander's law).
chunks.hook: COWS.

cards.q: Cold water in the right ear produces nystagmus beating which way?
cards.a: Left (cold opposite).

chunks.title: Infantile nystagmus & spasmus nutans
chunks.tldr: Starts in first months; horizontal, uniplanar, no oscillopsia, null point + head posture, damps on convergence, gone in sleep. Sensory (poor vision: cataract, albinism, LCA, ONH, achromatopsia) vs motor (X-linked, VA 6/12–6/36). Spasmus nutans: head nod + tilt + fine asymmetric nystagmus → image for glioma.
points: Bilateral poor vision before age 2 → nystagmus.
Motor: pendular primary, jerk on side gaze.
Spasmus nutans: 3–18 months; idiopathic resolves by 3 yrs; exclude chiasmal glioma, empty sella.
Latent nystagmus (with infantile ET): appears on covering one eye; fast phase toward uncovered eye.
chunks.hook: Nodding baby + wobbly eyes → MRI for glioma.

cards.q: Triad of spasmus nutans?
cards.a: Nystagmus (fine, asymmetric), head nodding, head tilt/torticollis.

chunks.title: Acquired nystagmus types
chunks.tldr: Downbeat = foramen magnum (Arnold–Chiari), lithium, phenytoin. Upbeat = posterior fossa, Wernicke. See-saw = parasellar (+ bitemporal hemianopia). PAN = cerebellar, reverses every 1–3 min. Convergence–retraction = Parinaud. Bruns = CP angle tumour.
points: Ataxic nystagmus: abducting eye in INO.
Bruns: coarse gaze-evoked towards lesion + fine vestibular away.
PAN: congenital, cerebellar, ataxia telangiectasia, phenytoin; baclofen helps.
Treatment: refraction/CLs, baclofen, gabapentin, botox, Kestenbaum-type surgery for null point.
Nystagmoid: flutter (horizontal), opsoclonus (all directions — neuroblastoma 'dancing eyes, dancing feet'), ocular bobbing (pontine haemorrhage).
SO myokymia: monocular oscillopsia; beta-blockers/carbamazepine.
chunks.hook: Downbeat = down at the foramen magnum. See-saw = sella.

cards.q: Classic location for downbeat nystagmus lesion?
cards.a: Cervicomedullary junction/foramen magnum (e.g. Arnold–Chiari).

cards.q: See-saw nystagmus suggests?
cards.a: Parasellar mass (often with bitemporal hemianopia).

chunks.title: Myasthenia gravis
chunks.tldr: Anti-AChR autoimmunity; fatigable weakness. Eye involved 90% (presenting 60%): variable ptosis (worse evening, sustained upgaze), Cogan lid twitch, any motility pattern. Tests: ice pack, AChR Ab (90% systemic, 50–70% ocular), MuSK, EMG, Tensilon. CT chest for thymoma (15%).
points: Women 2×; can mimic any palsy incl. pseudo-INO; pupils never involved.
Enhanced ptosis: lift one lid → other droops.
Ice test ~75% sensitive, highly specific.
Tensilon: atropine first; 2 mg then 8 mg; lasts ~5 min; risk bradycardia.
Associations: thyroid disease, RA, pernicious anaemia, SLE.
Avoid: aminoglycosides, macrolides, beta-blockers (incl. topical).
Rx: pyridostigmine, steroids, azathioprine; IVIG/plasmapheresis for crisis; thymectomy (75% improve).
Lambert–Eaton: presynaptic Ca channel Ab, lung cancer in 60%.
chunks.hook: Eyes tire by teatime → myasthenia. Pupils always spared.

cards.q: What is Cogan's lid twitch?
cards.a: Brief upward overshoot of the lid when the eyes saccade from downgaze to primary – myasthenia.

cards.q: Mandatory imaging in myasthenia?
cards.a: Chest CT/MRI for thymoma.

chunks.title: Myotonic dystrophy, CPEO, Kearns–Sayre & Miller Fisher
chunks.tldr: Myotonic dystrophy (DMPK, AD, anticipation): can't release grip, hatchet face, Christmas-tree cataract, ptosis, hypotony. CPEO: bilateral ptosis + symmetrical immobility, no diplopia. Kearns–Sayre: CPEO + heart block + salt-and-pepper retina, onset <20, ragged red fibres. Miller Fisher: ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia (anti-GQ1b).
points: Myotonic: frontal balding, cardiomyopathy, anaesthetic risk; polychromatic dust → stellate PSC.
CPEO: exposure risk with ptosis surgery; CK raised.
KSS: ECG and pacemaker; raised CSF protein.
OPMD (PABPN1): ptosis + dysphagia, middle age.
Miller Fisher = Guillain–Barré variant.
chunks.hook: Kearns–Sayre = 'Heart, Eyes, Retina' before 20.

cards.q: Classic triad of Kearns–Sayre syndrome?
cards.a: CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy, cardiac conduction defects (onset before 20).

cards.q: Antibody in Miller Fisher syndrome?
cards.a: Anti-GQ1b.

chunks.title: Neurofibromatosis 1 & 2
chunks.tldr: NF1 (chr 17, 1:4000): café-au-lait, axillary freckles, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules (95%), optic nerve glioma (15–40%), S-shaped lid plexiform neurofibroma, sphenoid wing absence → pulsating proptosis, choroidal nodules on OCT. NF2 (chr 22): bilateral acoustic neuromas, juvenile PSC cataract, ERM, combined hamartoma.
points: NF1: AD, 50% new mutations; learning difficulty, autism, MPNST.
Glaucoma (congenital, unilateral) with lid neurofibroma + hemifacial hypertrophy.
Choroidal hyper-reflective nodules on OCT/NIR in >80% (sensitive & specific).
Retinal corkscrew vessels; astrocytic hamartomas; ↑ melanoma risk with naevi.
NF2: Merlin; cataract before 30; ocular motor defects.
chunks.hook: NF1 = 17 letters in 'neurofibromatosis' (chr 17). NF2 = 2 ears (bilateral acoustic), chr 22.

cards.q: Ocular sign most specific for NF2?
cards.a: Juvenile posterior subcapsular/capsular cataract (also ERM, combined hamartoma).

cards.q: Cause of pulsating proptosis in NF1?
cards.a: Absence of the greater wing of sphenoid (spheno-orbital encephalocoele).

chunks.title: Migraine
chunks.tldr: Aura: binocular, hemifield, zig-zag fortification spectra spreading over 5–30 min (<60), then headache (or none). Without aura: unilateral throbbing 4–72 h, photophobia. Retinal migraine: monocular, rare — investigate like emboli. Prophylaxis: propranolol, topiramate, valproate, CGRP antibodies.
points: Women 18%, men 6%.
IHS aura criteria: reversible, builds >4 min, <60 min each, headache within 60 min.
Ophthalmoplegic migraine: kids, recurrent III palsy (demyelination).
Familial hemiplegic, basilar migraine.
Occipital epilepsy: coloured circles.
Acute: analgesics + metoclopramide; triptans, ergotamine.
Triggers: chocolate, cheese, alcohol, OCP, stress, sleep loss, fasting.
chunks.hook: Aura builds slowly and leaves in half an hour.

cards.q: Typical duration of migraine visual aura?
cards.a: 5–30 minutes (always <60).

cards.q: Why investigate 'retinal migraine'?
cards.a: It is monocular and may represent emboli/vasospasm; permanent loss can occur.

chunks.title: Neuralgias & eye pain mimics
chunks.tldr: Cluster: men, excruciating orbital pain 10 min–2 h, restless, tearing, red eye, Horner, same time nightly. SUNCT: seconds, many per day, red teary eye. Paroxysmal hemicrania: women, indomethacin-responsive. Trigeminal neuralgia: electric seconds, triggered, no autonomic signs → carbamazepine. Raeder: V1 pain + Horner → exclude dissection.
points: Migraine lies still in dark; cluster paces about.
Ice pick (primary stabbing) headache: sub-second jabs, benign.
HZO: pain 2–3 days before rash; zoster sine herpete.
Occipital neuralgia can spread to eye.
chunks.hook: Cluster = Clock-like, Crying eye, Can't sit still.

cards.q: Which headache responds dramatically to indomethacin?
cards.a: Paroxysmal hemicrania.

cards.q: Unilateral facial pain + Horner – urgent concern?
cards.a: Carotid dissection (Raeder paratrigeminal syndrome).

chunks.title: Blepharospasm & hemifacial spasm
chunks.tldr: Essential blepharospasm: bilateral, older women, worse with light/stress, gone in sleep; + jaw dystonia = Meige. Hemifacial spasm: unilateral, spreads down face → MRI (vessel compressing VII). Both: botulinum toxin every ~3 months (95% relief).
points: Exclude reflex blepharospasm (dry eye) and Parkinson.
Tinted glasses help.
Botox side effects: ptosis, lagophthalmos, dry eye, diplopia.
Myectomy if botox fails.
Orbicularis myokymia (lid twitch) = harmless.
chunks.hook: Both eyes = Blepharospasm. Half face = Hemifacial (scan it).

cards.q: Investigation for hemifacial spasm?
cards.a: MRI to exclude compression of the facial nerve (often vascular loop).

chunks.title: Circadian rhythm & space flight (SANS)
chunks.tldr: Melanopsin ganglion cells (blue ~480 nm) → retinohypothalamic tract → suprachiasmatic nucleus → pineal melatonin. Blindness, dense cataract, advanced glaucoma, RP disturb sleep → melatonin, cataract surgery helps. SANS: long space flights → disc oedema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, hyperopic shift.
points: ~⅔ of astronauts on >6-month missions lose some VA.
Cause: cephalad fluid shift in microgravity.
chunks.hook: Blue light tells the brain it's daytime.

cards.q: Which retinal cells drive circadian rhythm?
cards.a: Intrinsically photosensitive (melanopsin) retinal ganglion cells.
